ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Informed consent was obtained and all aspects of the study were approved by the University of North Carolina's institutional review board.
Subjects were generally regular SFV users, which may influence engagement and neural responses in ways distinct from a user's first time on the app.
Informed consent was obtained and all aspects of the study were approved by the University of North Carolina's institutional review board.
Subjects were instructed to sit and stare at the off iPhone screen.

Subjects were given a lab iPhone with the TikTok app loaded, and instructed to scroll and view videos as follows: "Scroll as you normally would if this were your own brand-new TikTok account, but only stay on the For You page.
When time was up, participants were told they could stop viewing, the researcher stopped the screen recording, and the fNIRS recording was ended.
Subjects were asked on conclusion of the task to rate on a 1-7 Likert scale: 1) "For the first 5 minutes of scrolling, how personally relevant did the content feel?"
Immediately after the naive algorithm task, subjects were presented with three 5-minute clips from their session, close to the first, middle, and last 5 minutes of their scrolling.

Using a set of interactive buttons that could be turned on and off during the clips, subjects were instructed to label how they had felt during that part of the TikTok scrolling task, trying their best to reflect on how they had felt on initial viewing rather than in the current moment rewatching the clips.
Subjects were excluded from analysis if they had valid data in less than 50% of channels in any ROI.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = 0.907", Sentence = "This effect was not observed for the temporal lobe model (F(3, 4809) = 0.18, p = 0.907)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Personalized recommender algorithms are among the most influential design features of modern digital platforms, continuously adapting content in response to user behavior.
Yet, little is known about how the brain responds as personalized digital environments emerge over time.

To examine neural activity during this process, we used functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to develop a highly ecologically valid paradigm where 72 young adults scrolled on new accounts for a short-form video platform for 35 minutes while recommendation algorithms adapted content to their individual preferences.
Participants reported that content was significantly more personally relevant by the end of scrolling, and durations of felt boredom significantly decreased.

Despite all encountering unique content and scrolling at their own pace, participants who reported greater perceived personalization exhibited distinct trajectories of prefrontal and temporal neural connectivity, and these trajectories varied by problematic social media use.

Among participants reporting higher problematic social media use, successful personalization was associated with increasing intra-prefrontal connectivity, suggesting that shifts in cortical dynamics during personalization may be relevant to vulnerability for pathological use.

To our knowledge, this study provides the first in vivo evidence on how neural systems dynamically adapt alongside personalizing digital environments, and that this adaptive trajectory varies as a function of problematic social media use.

More broadly, these findings demonstrate that neural adaptation to algorithmic personalization can be measured during actual deviceusage, providing a framework for studying brain responses to real-world digital experiences.

Personalized algorithms dominantly shape what people see and engage with online, yet, we have previously not studied how brain dynamics shift alongside real-time algorithmic personalization to individual user preferences.

We provide the first in vivo evidence that neural systems dynamically adapt alongside algorithmic personalization and that these trajectories differ according to vulnerability for problematic social media use.

The ability to find meaningful neural signal while all participants engage with the app in different manners demonstrates the feasibility of studying how the brain adapts to digital technology use in real-time with highly ecologically valid paradigms.
The design features of social media are crafted to be engaging in manners directly related to natural biases in our psychological and neural processing of social and reward stimuli 1 .

text.text: Yet, we still have little direct data on how the brain responds as platforms actively adapt to user preference.
Algorithmic personalization has vastly changed how we navigate digital spaces.
Over the past decade, media platforms have shifted away from feeds based on user-selected content or temporal order 5, 6 .

text.text: Previous work has found notable differences in neural responses to short form video content recommended by personalized algorithms versus generically obtained social media content.

Personally recommended videos elicit more connectivity between regions implicated in self-referential and social processing, including the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC), ventral lateral prefrontal cortex, and the temporal parietal junction (TPJ) 12 .

text.text: Overall, recommender algorithms appear to modulate nodes important to the broader defaultmode network (DMN), possibly due to self-referential processing becoming acutely focused on the presented video content.
Yet, these effects are not likely to be static.
Algorithmic personalization emerges gradually during scrolling, and as such, we should expect these prefrontal and temporal regions to dynamically change in response.
When users first download a SFV app they are exposed to a naïve recommender system.
The recommender algorithms of SFV apps are tuned to get new users to become habitual users, meaning this initial calibration is essential to establishing future patterns of use 10, 14, 15 .
text.formatted: The recommender algorithms of SFV apps are tuned to get new users to become habitual users, meaning this initial calibration is essential to establishing future patterns of use <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> .

text.text: This calibration period may be especially consequential for individuals vulnerable to problematic SFV use, as personalized recommendations may amplify preexisting tendencies toward excessive engagement.
Importantly, social media does not affect all users in the same way, and there is individual variation in susceptibility to problematic engagement 16 .
text.formatted: Importantly, social media does not affect all users in the same way, and there is individual variation in susceptibility to problematic engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> .

text.text: Prior work suggests that traits associated with problematic SFV use, such as heightened sensitivity to self-relevant content and lower self-concept clarity, may lead users to become more easily immersed into SFV apps 17 .
text.formatted: Prior work suggests that traits associated with problematic SFV use, such as heightened sensitivity to self-relevant content and lower self-concept clarity, may lead users to become more easily immersed into SFV apps <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> .

text.text: As personalized feeds increasingly align with individual interests, users with vulnerabilities such as this may be especially likely to experience a greater sense of immersion and engagement, leading to problematic use.

Neurally, adults with higher problematic SFV use exhibit different patterns of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) connectivity in which the DLPFC is preferentially embedded within higher-order association networks as opposed to sensory and attention networks 18, 19 .
text.formatted: Neurally, adults with higher problematic SFV use exhibit different patterns of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) connectivity in which the DLPFC is preferentially embedded within higher-order association networks as opposed to sensory and attention networks <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> .

text.text: These associations represent important relationships between problematic SFV use and neural/psychological processing, but they do not capture how neural responses evolve, as content becomes increasingly personalized, in vivo.
How the brain responds to a feed of content that is becoming more personalized is foundational to understanding how, and for whom, addictive patterns of engagement emerge.
Traditional neuroimaging paradigms often rely on standardized stimuli presentations that provide limited opportunity for users to selectively engage with content.
More importantly, highly controlled stimulus sets are not designed to capture algorithmic tuning, whereby content becomes increasingly personalized through continuous user feedback.

This limitation speaks to a broader challenge in the field: real-world experiences are often defined by evolving, irregular, timecourses for experiences which are near impossible to model in controlled stimuli 20 .
text.formatted: This limitation speaks to a broader challenge in the field: real-world experiences are often defined by evolving, irregular, timecourses for experiences which are near impossible to model in controlled stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> .

text.text: Functional nearinfrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), a portable neuroimaging method, has previously been used to study unique affordances of real-world media contexts, finding distinct patterns of activation in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) during social media scrolling compared to television viewing and gaming 18 ; this highlights the importance of treating digital media not as purely an audiovisual stimuli but as an interactive experience 21 .
text.formatted: Functional nearinfrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), a portable neuroimaging method, has previously been used to study unique affordances of real-world media contexts, finding distinct patterns of activation in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) during social media scrolling compared to television viewing and gaming <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> ; this highlights the importance of treating digital media not as purely an audiovisual stimuli but as an interactive experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> .

text.text: As such, we took advantage of fNIRS's greater ecological validity to develop a highly naturalistic study on algorithmic personalization, allowing individuals to scroll on an actual smartphone device while neural connectivity is measured in real time.
In the present study, we used fNIRS to examine dynamic functional connectivity while 72 users naturally scrolled on a naïve short-form video account for 35 minutes.
This paradigm allows us to investigate the varying neural trajectories of users in real time as the algorithm personalizes to their preferences.
We hypothesized that prefronto-temporal and intra-prefrontal connectivity would increase over the course of scrolling, depending on how personalized the content felt to users by the end.

Further, we predicted that this relationship would vary as a function of problematic social media use, such that individuals with higher problematic use would show larger increases in connectivity as content became increasingly personalized, reflecting more recruitment of these self-relevant networks due to their heightened vulnerability to be 'captured' by the flow state of the app.

After scrolling for 35 minutes, we asked participants to rate how personally relevant the videos they were shown felt during the first 5 minutes of scrolling and during the last 5 minutes of scrolling on a 1-7 Likert scale (1= "Not relevant at all",7= "Completely relevant").
We tested the difference in these subjective ratings of personal relevance as a manipulation check to ensure that the paradigm was successful.
Personal relevance was significantly higher by the end of scrolling (M = 4.29, SD =1.51) compared to the first 5 minutes of scrolling (M = 1.81, SD =1.06; t= 12.21, p<0.001, Cohen's d= 1.44).
text.formatted: Personal relevance was significantly higher by the end of scrolling (M = 4.29, SD =1.51) compared to the first 5 minutes of scrolling (M = 1.81, SD =1.06; t= 12.21, p<0.001, Cohen's d= 1.44).

text.text: This finding demonstrates that the recommender algorithm substantially increased the perceived relevance of video content to individual users.
Notably, there was meaningful variation in the extent to which personal relevance increased for participants.

Due to this variability, we used the personal relevance rating as moderator in our subsequent analyses of how neural connectivity changed over time, and how these trajectories differed based on problematic social media use.
Using screen recordings, we had subjects annotate how they felt during the first 5 minutes of scrolling, 20-25 minutes in, and 30-35 minutes in.
The 20 minute timepoint was chosen as an estimate of when the algorithm may be adapted to personal preferences if this occurs more quickly than 30 minutes.
Across all 5 minute windows of annotated videos, the most commonly reported feeling was interest, which was reported for an average of 104.43 seconds across all segments.
Other commonly reported feelings were amusement (M=96.21 seconds), boredom (M=70.21 seconds), and happiness (M=41.21 seconds).

Nostalgia (M=17.50 seconds), awe (M=17.15 seconds), sadness (M=12.75 seconds), and disgust (M=9.55 seconds) were generally reported for shorter durations, though still were reported in the majority of annotated segments (~59%, 56%, 51% and 50% respectively).
Anger was rare, being reported in less than half of all segments (~34%, (M=5.77seconds).
We used mixed linear effects models to test differences in affect duration between the first, second, and third annotated segments of videos so that random intercepts for subjects could be included.
Subjects experienced significantly shorter durations of boredom in the second (β= -21.20, p=0.016), and last segment (β=-17.64, p=0.045) compared to the first.
Participants also reported significantly more amusement in the last segment compared to the first segment (β=21.39, p=0.042).
No other duration differences in affect between segments reached significance (Figure 2).
text.formatted: No other duration differences in affect between segments reached significance (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Longitudinal mixed-effects models with natural splines (3 degrees of freedom) and subject-specific random slopes were used to model nonlinear changes in connectivity over time (Table S1).
text.formatted: Longitudinal mixed-effects models with natural splines (3 degrees of freedom) and subject-specific random slopes were used to model nonlinear changes in connectivity over time (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>).

text.text: An omnibus Wald F-test was used to test the non-linear effects of time.

Dynamic functional connectivity significantly changed over time in the intra-prefrontal (F(3, 29064) = 8.13, p < 0.001), prefrontal-temporal (F(3, 38916) = 16.89, p < 0.001), and temporal lobe models (F(3, 4809) = 3.55, p = 0.014) (Table 1).
text.formatted: Dynamic functional connectivity significantly changed over time in the intra-prefrontal (F(3, 29064) = 8.13, p < 0.001), prefrontal-temporal (F(3, 38916) = 16.89, p < 0.001), and temporal lobe models (F(3, 4809) = 3.55, p = 0.014) (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Both the intra-prefrontal and prefrontal-temporal models showed significant three-way interactions between time, problematic social media use, and perceived personalization by the end of scrolling (intra-prefrontal: F(3, 29064) = 5.19, p = 0.001; prefrontaltemporal: F(3, 38916) = 3.21, p = 0.022).
This effect was not observed for the temporal lobe model (F(3, 4809) = 0.18, p = 0.907).
For intra-prefrontal connectivity, perceived personalization exhibited a crossover pattern across levels of problematic social media use (Figure 3).
text.formatted: For intra-prefrontal connectivity, perceived personalization exhibited a crossover pattern across levels of problematic social media use (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

text.text: Among participants endorsing less problematic social media use, greater personalization was associated with relatively lower intraprefrontal connectivity across much of the scrolling session compared with lower personalization.

In contrast, among participants reporting higher problematic social media use, greater personalization was associated with relatively higher intra-prefrontal connectivity during the latter half of the session.

Thus, the association between perceived personalization and intra-prefrontal connectivity differed across levels of problematic social media use, such that greater personalization was associated with lower connectivity among those with lower problematic social media use but higher connectivity among those with higher problematic social media use.
For prefrontal-temporal connectivity, participants with higher problematic social media use exhibited higher connectivity at the beginning of the scrolling task (Figure 3).
text.formatted: For prefrontal-temporal connectivity, participants with higher problematic social media use exhibited higher connectivity at the beginning of the scrolling task (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

text.text: Connectivity trajectories varied as a function of perceived personalization success, particularly among participants reporting higher problematic social media use.
Among these participants, those reporting greater personalization success showed an overall sustained decline in prefrontal-temporal connectivity across the scrolling session.
In contrast, participants reporting lower personalization success exhibited a nonlinear trajectory characterized by an initial decline followed by a later rebound.
As a result, trajectories increasingly diverged across the session, with the high-personalization group exhibiting lower prefrontal-temporal connectivity during the later portions of scrolling.
This study uses a novel, naturalistic paradigm to study how algorithmic tuning of content affects neural processes as it unfolds in real time.
The self-report data on personalization confirmed the effectiveness and speed of short-form video feed algorithms at tuning to user preference.

While the reports of personalization reflect the first and last 5 minutes of the 35 minute paradigm, the affect labelling data suggests that a significant shift likely occurred well before 30 minutes.
By 20-25 minutes into scrolling, subjects reported boredom significantly less often.
Our findings further show that the perceived success of algorithmic personalization is associated with neural trajectories diverging within approximately 20 minutes of scrolling.

More broadly, this period of algorithmic calibration represents a laboratory analogue of the real-world process through which social media platforms progressively increase user engagement and, for some individuals, contribute to problematic patterns of use.
These neural trajectories depended on individual differences in problematic social media use, suggesting different vulnerabilities to digital engagement.

Participants reporting more problematic social media exhibited connectivity trajectories consistent with increasing segregation of prefrontal and temporal processing as content become more personalized.
The specificity of this diverging trajectory to individual variation in problematic social media use is notable, as the majority of the sample used SFV apps on at least a daily basis.
Of methodological significance, these temporal patterns were uncovered despite all subjects encountering unique video content, and all scrolling at their own pace.

This study is the first evidence of how the organization of cortical networks shift during real-world algorithmic personalization and gives insight into how distinct processing of personally relevant content may facilitate excessive and problematic use.
Our neural connectivity data, measured on a continuous sliding-window basis, demonstrated noticeably diverging patterns related to personalization success possibly as early as 10 minutes in.

Although the reported personalization success used in the models is only a retrospective reflection specific to the last 5 minutes of content, its association with connectivity trajectories this early suggests that the effectiveness of algorithmic tuning is reflected in psychological and neural processes well before.

Individual susceptibilities to algorithmic personalization may also play a role in this early stage-setting, as shown by problematic social media use's association with personalization-related neural trajectories.

The neural connectivity results align with previous fMRI studies finding that personalized SFV content preferentially engages dorsomedial prefrontal and broader default mode network systems relative to generic content 13 .
text.formatted: The neural connectivity results align with previous fMRI studies finding that personalized SFV content preferentially engages dorsomedial prefrontal and broader default mode network systems relative to generic content <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> .

text.text: These regions are thought to support self-referential processing, social cognition, and the integration of personally relevant information.

Personalized short-form video content has previously been associated with greater recruitment of dorsomedial prefrontal DMN pathways and stronger coupling between self-referential and attentional systems, suggesting that algorithmic recommendations increase the personal significance of viewed content 12 .
text.formatted: Personalized short-form video content has previously been associated with greater recruitment of dorsomedial prefrontal DMN pathways and stronger coupling between self-referential and attentional systems, suggesting that algorithmic recommendations increase the personal significance of viewed content <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: Our findings extend this work by demonstrating that these neural differences are not simply static properties of relevant versus irrelevant media content, but dynamically emerge during the process through which recommender systems learn user preferences.

This pattern was most pronounced among individuals reporting greater problematic social media use, for whom successful personalization was associated with opposing changes in intra-prefrontal and prefrontal-temporal connectivity trajectories.
Specifically, greater personalization success was associated with relatively higher intra-prefrontal connectivity and lower prefrontal-temporal connectivity over the course of scrolling.
This pattern is consistent with a reorganization of cortical network dynamics during algorithmic personalization.
Shifts in prefrontal-temporal connectivity are broadly consistent with previous literature on DMN alterations in problematic social media use, though fNIRS does not cover the entirety of the DMN.
Resting-state studies have demonstrated that people with problematic internet use exhibited altered inter-network and intranetwork functional connectivity of the DMN 22, 23 .
text.formatted: Resting-state studies have demonstrated that people with problematic internet use exhibited altered inter-network and intranetwork functional connectivity of the DMN <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> .

text.text: Work specific to problematic SFV use has found altered patterns of DLPFC connectivity -a well covered region in our fNIRS montage.

In a partial parallel to our results, DLPFC-dorsal anterior cingulate connectivity increases during personally recommended short form videos, broadly mirroring our finding of increased intra-frontal connectivity 24 .
text.formatted: In a partial parallel to our results, DLPFC-dorsal anterior cingulate connectivity increases during personally recommended short form videos, broadly mirroring our finding of increased intra-frontal connectivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> .

text.text: Another study also found prefrontal decoupling from sensory and attention-related regions during short-form videos compared to longer videos in the learning context 25 .
text.formatted: Another study also found prefrontal decoupling from sensory and attention-related regions during short-form videos compared to longer videos in the learning context <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> .

text.text: Mechanistically, our results may suggest that individuals prone to problematic use may process increasingly personally relevant content in a more segregated manner, with regions important to integration such as key prefrontal nodes communicating more amongst themselves than within a cross-network cortical system.
This study has limitations.
Subjects were generally regular SFV users, which may influence engagement and neural responses in ways distinct from a user's first time on the app.
Personalization was measured through self-reported relevance of the content during the first and last 5 minutes of scrolling, which may not fully represent the 35 minutes of scrolling.

Future studies could use more objective and detailed measures of personalization, such as comparing content categories between the novel scrolling task and the subject's personal short-form video app account, or behavioral metrics such as changes in swiping speed.

Similarly, affect was retrospectively measured in three 5 minute video segments to balance subject-level specificity with participant burden. fNIRS's mobile nature and flexibility allows the ecological validity necessary for this study, but it cannot give a full neurobiological picture of personalization processes.
Many important regions of the DMN, as well as all subcortical regions, are not measurable through fNIRS.
These regions likely play an important role in algorithmic capture based on previous literature on social media use and personalized content.

More broadly, our study uses a short-form video app algorithm as a prominent and widely used example of personalization in the real-world, but this type of algorithmic tuning extends beyond video platforms, to shaping behavior on social media apps, AI chatbots, e-commerce, and even health and learning platforms.
As recommender systems are implemented into more technologies, understanding how they shape brains has implications beyond any specific media platform.

Despite these limitations and the further work which needs to be done, one of the most novel aspects of the present study is our ability to observe the brain in real time as a naive shortform video account is progressively shaped by the platform's personalization algorithms.

Rather than treating the social media environment as static exposure, our approach captures the dynamic co-evolution of the digital environment and the brain's responses to it as the algorithm learns about the user.

This provides a rare window into the neural correlates of personalization as it unfolds in real-time, allowing us to simultaneously watch change in the digital environment and the resulting neural adaptation.

It also should be highlighted that temporal neural trends related to personalization and problematic social media use were found despite all subjects having individualized, uncontrolled, streams of content shown to them.

As the field of neuroimaging has evolved, we have gradually made progress toward paradigms that better capture real-world experiences by sacrificing some experimental control, including reliance on averaged activity, strict standardization of stimuli, consistency of content exposure, and attempts to minimize variability in affective responses across participants [26] [27] [28] [29] .
text.formatted: As the field of neuroimaging has evolved, we have gradually made progress toward paradigms that better capture real-world experiences by sacrificing some experimental control, including reliance on averaged activity, strict standardization of stimuli, consistency of content exposure, and attempts to minimize variability in affective responses across participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref> .

text.text: This study demonstrates that neuroimaging paradigms can successfully accommodate all of these naturalistic necessities, even in combination, while still identifying scientifically useful insights.
Our data demonstrate that the success of algorithmic personalization is associated with measurable changes in neural processing that emerge within minutes of use.
These trajectories differed as a function of problematic social media use, suggesting that personalization's effects on neural processing may depend on individual vulnerabilities.
A neuroscience that can abstract trends across highly individualized experiences is critical for deriving ecologically valid insights into how algorithmic systems influence affect and behavior.
We collected data from 80 college-aged subjects, all of which currently, or had in the past, used short-form video apps.
Informed consent was obtained and all aspects of the study were approved by the University of North Carolina's institutional review board.

Of these subjects, 8 were removed due to having poor quality data in too many fNIRS channels (see Pre-processing and Dynamic functional connectivity sections) leaving a main sample of 72 participants (Table 2).
text.formatted: Of these subjects, 8 were removed due to having poor quality data in too many fNIRS channels (see Pre-processing and Dynamic functional connectivity sections) leaving a main sample of 72 participants (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Over 93% of participants reported using TikTok or Instagram Reels, two of the most popular SFV apps, at least once a day.
All data were collected using a 16x16 NIRSport system (NIRx Medical Technologies).
Participants' head size was measured so that an appropriately sized cap could be selected.
Changes in oxygenated (HbO) and deoxygenated hemoglobin (HbR) were measured with a 48channel montage across bilateral frontal and temporoparietal cortices.
We additionally had 8 short-channels for capturing confound signals (Figure S1).
text.formatted: We additionally had 8 short-channels for capturing confound signals (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref>).

text.text: We used a sampling rate of 7 Hz.
Before data collection, signal quality was checked for each channel, and optodes were adjusted until good quality was achieved.
We used TikTok as the short-form video app in the study.
The TikTok accounts on lab smartphones were reset before every new data collection, and efforts were taken to limit or eliminate accumulated data from modifying the TikTok algorithm between sessions.
Sessions were run with two different iPhone and four email-based TikTok accounts, rotating phones and accounts to always use the least recently used one.
The only initial demographic information in these accounts was a generic date of birth set to indicate a 20 year old, aligning with our targeted sample of 18-24 year olds.
After each data collection, multiple steps were taken to reset the algorithm to a naive state as much as transparently possible.
First, all videos 'liked' in the previous session were manually un-liked.
In the "Activity Center" of the TikTok app, watch history, comment history, and search history were all deleted.
In Settings and Privacy-> Ad preferences of the phone itself, "off-TikTok data" was disabled to prevent TikTok from using data from other apps to inform ad selection.
text.formatted: In Settings and Privacy-> Ad preferences of the phone itself, "off-TikTok data" was disabled to prevent TikTok from using data from other apps to inform ad selection.

text.text: Within Settings and Privacy, the cache was cleared for Tiktok.
Finally, the TikTok app would be re-opened and "Refresh you Feed" would be selected within Content Preferences.
A 5-minute resting-state recording was performed to be used as a control variable in analyses.
Subjects were instructed to sit and stare at the off iPhone screen.

Reporting and user data analysis by the Washington Post found that TikTok's algorithm can generally personalize content to an effective enough extent to increase future use durations in approximately 30 minutes of scrolling 15 .
text.formatted: Reporting and user data analysis by the Washington Post found that TikTok's algorithm can generally personalize content to an effective enough extent to increase future use durations in approximately 30 minutes of scrolling <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> .

text.text: As such, we made our paradigm 35 minutes long to attempt to capture this window of algorithmic tuning.

Subjects were given a lab iPhone with the TikTok app loaded, and instructed to scroll and view videos as follows: "Scroll as you normally would if this were your own brand-new TikTok account, but only stay on the For You page.

You can do anything on the For You page, like watching, scrolling, skipping videos, and looking at comments -whatever feels natural to you, as we just want to see how you'd typically explore and interact with the feed."
The researcher would begin screen recording on the iPhone while hitting an initial trigger for fNIRS recording, then hand it to the participant telling them not to begin scrolling until told.

The researcher would then tell the subject to begin scrolling while sending a second trigger, marking a starting point in the neural data for the session that the data could be trimmed to begin at the first scroll in the screen recording.
A silent timer was then started for 35 minutes.
When time was up, participants were told they could stop viewing, the researcher stopped the screen recording, and the fNIRS recording was ended.
Subjects were asked on conclusion of the task to rate on a 1-7 Likert scale: 1) "For the first 5 minutes of scrolling, how personally relevant did the content feel?"
and 2) "For the last 5 minutes of scrolling, how personally relevant did the content feel?".
Immediately after the naive algorithm task, subjects were presented with three 5-minute clips from their session, close to the first, middle, and last 5 minutes of their scrolling.
Of our 72 participants with valid fNIRS data, 59 participated in this emotion annotation.

To assure rapid processing of these videos clips while also excluding seconds at the beginning and end of the screen recording which were not during the 35 minute scrolling duration, the first clip was started at 60 seconds into the recording, the middle at 1260 seconds, and the last at 360 seconds before the end of the recording (to exclude the final 60 seconds).
We used the publicly available Cinemotion tool (https://github.com/jtkaplan/cinemotion) to allow subjects to retrospectively report their emotional state during the task.
text.formatted: We used the publicly available Cinemotion tool (<ref type="url" target="https://github.com/jtkaplan/cinemotion">https://github.com/jtkaplan/cinemotion</ref>) to allow subjects to retrospectively report their emotional state during the task.

text.text: Using a set of interactive buttons that could be turned on and off during the clips, subjects were instructed to label how they had felt during that part of the TikTok scrolling task, trying their best to reflect on how they had felt on initial viewing rather than in the current moment rewatching the clips.
Subjects could turn 9 different emotion labels on and off (happy, amused, interested, sad, angry, bored, disgusted, nostalgic, awed), and multiple labels could be on at the same time.
An additional "All off" button was present to turn off all current labels.

We aimed to pick a set of labels encompassing positive, negative, and potentially mixed valence, while also best representing emotional states that were likely to be frequent during SFV viewing (hence, excluding otherwise typically measured states such as fear).

The Cinemotion tool generates time logs indicating when buttons were turned on and off, which were then used to calculate reported emotion durations for each of the three segments, as well as the total number of times subjects transitioned between emotion states (indicated by any change in a button to 'on' or 'off').
Participants in the study completed a battery of survey measures.
Relevant to the current analysis, problematic social media use was assessed using the 9-item Social Media Disorder scale 30 .
text.formatted: Relevant to the current analysis, problematic social media use was assessed using the 9-item Social Media Disorder scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30</ref> .

text.text: The scale is based on addictive disorder criteria from the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders 5th edition, with each of the 9 items being endorsed or not.
A score of 0-1 is generally considered normative behavior, 2-4 indicates potentially risky usage, and 5 or more is considered pathological use or "disordered".
In our sample, roughly even proportions fell into normative and risky ranges (47.2% and 45.8% respectively) while 6.9% endorsed 5 or more items.
NIRS data were preprocessed to remove physiological noise and head motion artifacts using Satori 2.2.4 31 .
text.formatted: NIRS data were preprocessed to remove physiological noise and head motion artifacts using Satori 2.2.4 <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31</ref> .

text.text: First, we trimmed data to the length of the rest (300 seconds) and TikTok (2100 seconds) periods.
Raw data were converted to optical density data.
Then, channels were rejected and removed if their scalp coupling index (SCI) was below 0.7.
Motion correction was applied using temporal derivative distribution repair 32 .
text.formatted: Motion correction was applied using temporal derivative distribution repair <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32</ref> .

text.text: Using the modified Beer-Lambert law, optical density data was converted to concentration changes of HbO and HbR.
We then applied short channel regression to remove physiological noise, using all available short channels after channel rejection 33 .
text.formatted: We then applied short channel regression to remove physiological noise, using all available short channels after channel rejection <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref> .

text.text: A Butterworth bandpass filter was applied with cutoff frequencies of 0.1 Hz and 0.009 Hz.
Data were visually inspected to assess signal quality at each step.
HbO values for each channel, in each subject, were extracted.
Channels were grouped into regions of interest (ROIs) for subsequent dynamic connectivity analyses (see Table S2).
text.formatted: Channels were grouped into regions of interest (ROIs) for subsequent dynamic connectivity analyses (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">S2</ref>).

text.text: Subjects were excluded from analysis if they had valid data in less than 50% of channels in any ROI.

Because of the high rate of drop-out of channels in the superior parietal area (~10% of the sample would be excluded if required to have the superior parietal ROIs), we excluded these ROIs from further analysis.
Overall, this led to a final sample of 72 participants with complete fNIRS data and personalization data.
Dynamic functional connectivity was calculated using a sliding window approach, with windows being 60 seconds long (420 timepoints) and with 30 second steps (210 timepoints) between each window.
For each pair of regions of interest in each window, Pearson's correlations were calculated for each pairwise combination of valid channels in each ROI.
Correlations were converted to Fisher's z statistics, which were then averaged for the overall connectivity of that window.
Statistical modelling was performed in R using the Non-Linear Mixed Effects package (nlme) 34 .
text.formatted: Statistical modelling was performed in R using the Non-Linear Mixed Effects package (nlme) <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34</ref> .

text.text: The 15 pairwise ROI combinations of dynamic connectivity were grouped into three separate models: 1) intra-prefrontal connectivity, 2) intra-temporal lobe connectivity, 3) prefrontaltemporal lobe connectivity.

Since the first and third models involved more than one pair of ROIs, specific ROI-ROI pair was included as an independent variable in these models, so each model could broadly be considered to predict connectivity of these intra and inter-lobe dynamics.
We used longitudinal linear mixed-effects models to characterize changes in connectivity over time.
Time was modelled using natural splines with 3 degrees of freedom to allow for nonlinear trajectories.

Additional fixed effects of the model included ROI pair, post-scrolling personalization, early scrolling personalization (to account for baseline content relevance before algorithm shaping), the interaction between post-personalization and time, and average resting-state connectivity for the corresponding pair of ROIs.
Subject-specific random slopes were included.

To best account for the temporal dependence, including that introduced by the 50% overlap in adjacent connectivity windows, a first-order autoregressive residual correlation structure was specified for each ROI pair within each subject.
